content: 1. Pulsus tardus et parvus, also referred to as pulsus parvus et tardus or commonly known as a slow-rising or anacrotic pulse, is a clinical sign characterized by a weak (parvus) and delayed (tardus) pulse when palpated, relative to the contraction of the heart. This finding is classically associated with aortic valve stenosis. In the context of aortic stenosis, typical clinical findings include a narrow pulse pressure, a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space with radiation to the carotid arteries, and a delayed, slow-rising carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus). 2. Pulsus bisferiens, also known as a bisferious or biphasic pulse, is a clinical sign where a double peak per cardiac cycle can be appreciated upon palpation of the pulse. The term bisferious translates to striking twice. This finding is classically observed in cases of aortic insufficiency coexisting with aortic stenosis. It may also be present in isolated but severe aortic insufficiency or in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. 3. Pulsus bigeminus is a cardiovascular phenomenon characterized by pairs of two heartbeats occurring close together, followed by a longer pause. The second pulse in each pair is weaker than the first. This pattern is typically caused by premature ventricular contractions occurring after every other beat. Pulsus bigeminus can be a sign of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy or other forms of heart disease, but it may also occur as an innocent and transient phenomenon. 4. Pulsus paradoxus, also referred to as paradoxic pulse or paradoxical pulse, is an exaggerated decrease in the strength of the pulse during the inspiratory phase of respiration. During inspiration, the pulse becomes weaker, and during expiration, it becomes stronger. This phenomenon is often seen in conditions such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The paradox in pulsus paradoxus lies in the clinical observation that extra beats can be detected on cardiac auscultation during inspiration, which are not palpable at the radial pulse. This results from an accentuated drop in blood pressure, leading to the radial pulse becoming impalpable. It may also be accompanied by an increase in jugular venous pressure (Kussmaul sign). As is typical during inspiration, the heart rate increases due to enhanced venous return.
